Quick update from infra: the kernel tweak was live only on our canary hosts, but an autoscaling policy mislabel caused a small subset of Nimbus traffic to be pinned to a canary pool (approx 3% of requests). That aligns with the timing and the spike shape.

What I recommend (fast path):
1) Immediate: route all Nimbus production traffic for clinical-triage to halo-1.1 (stable) for the next 6 hours while we validate canary isolation. This is safe — halo-1.1 provides equivalent clinical accuracy per our evals.
2) Short term: patch autoscaler tag filter and rebootstrap canary hosts (30–45min).
3) Postmortem: run a focused eval comparing halo-1.2 latency at typical sequence lengths and re-evaluate kernel gating.

I've attached a short playbook for fallback activation.

Monica
Monica Patel

Elena / team — thanks. From a commercial/customer-experience angle, two options for Nimbus during the next 24 hours:

A) Fallback routing to halo-1.1 (recommended): we keep feature parity and avoid timeouts. No invoice adjustments required; we log an SLA incident for tracking.
B) Keep on halo-1.2 with a soft traffic cap (80%) while we remediate: lower risk to model drift but may see degraded responsiveness in the UI and potential demo impact.

If Nimbus wants a formal SLA grace window or credit for the disruption, we can escalate to account execs; historically, we reserve credits for verified outages (p95 exceedance affecting >5% of traffic for >30m). Given Monica's estimate that ~3% of requests were affected and that we can route away quickly, I suggest option A and a proactive incident postmortem.

I'll stand by to coordinate messaging for the customer-facing incident note.

Ben Carter
Enterprise Account Executive, Redwood Inference
